en: "And all those who do not know that reality are fruitless. Therefore, reality is introduced. What is that reality? It is the bodhicitta, which is primordially unarisen and quiescent, as stated by the Blessed One in the *Samājottaravyākhyāyitantra*:
"Without beginning or end, quiescent, the exhaustion of existence and non-existence, all-pervading..."
The inseparability of emptiness and compassion is known as bodhicitta.

And since this is not accomplished apart from the isolations of body, speech, and mind, that [process] is introduced. In that regard, the practitioner, having removed ordinary ego-grasping through conviction in emptiness, [visualizes] himself instantaneously in the form of Mahāvajradhara, white in color, with two arms, and so forth. Thus, up to the end [of the passage]: "The yogi who performs the four yogas, having meditated upon the syllable *hūṃ* as his core, having seen the world, and having arisen as the Vajrasattva of the world and its origin, should move about with that wisdom as prescribed."

The isolation of the body (*kāyaviveka*) is the thorough knowledge that the body of Vajradhara—which consists of perceived mantras—is unreal, by virtue of its being the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvasvabhāvatva*). According to the scripture stating, "Families (*kula*) are said to be of a hundred kinds," unreality is established through worldly convention alone, because the intrinsic nature of the states of childhood, youth, and old age is not perceived. Therefore, the isolation of the body is the unreality of the body situated within the three realms, established through both scripture and realization, just like [the unreality] of a body reflected on the surface of water.

"Containing the syllable *hūṃ*" means that it arises from the three syllables. Having understood the unreality (*alīkatva*) of the body, how can the unreality of its cause—the three syllables—be otherwise? In this regard, it is not known without following the sequence of the reality of wind (*vāyutattva*). The "reality of wind" refers to the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*). It consists of twenty-one thousand six hundred [breaths] through the processes of entry, abiding, and emergence from the two nostrils in the sequence of the four mandalas. Regarding those [processes] such as entry and so forth, there is the symbolic mantra recitation: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*.

Through its cultivation, one should contemplate a mustard seed at the tip of the nose; within that mustard seed, one should contemplate the entire world with its moving and non-moving beings, and so forth, until reaching the ultimate limit of excellence. Through the cessation of sixteen hundred and twenty thousand [breaths], there occurs the cessation even of the three syllables; thus, the unreality of speech is the isolation of speech (*vāgviveka*), just as in the case of an echo.

In this very sequence, because the mind—which consists of the grasped, the grasper, and the act of grasping—is conjoined with the vital wind (*vāyu*), even its effects—the one hundred and sixty innate natures (*prakṛti*) such as detachment, attachment, and intermediate attachment—are unreal; this is the discernment of the mind (*cittaviveka*). Just as it is with the dream-mind, so too, through the second method of vajra-recitation, by thoroughly knowing the lack of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*) in the nature of speech and mind, those very innate natures—the sixty-two views and the ninety-eight afflictions (*kleśa*)—[are likewise unreal].
